title: Quantum error correction well below the color code threshold
authors: Ali Lavasani, Adam P. Reed, Joan M. Dreiling, Annie J. Park, Michael Mills, Matteo Puviani, Gabriel Matos, M. S. Allman, Noah Berthusen, Natalie C. Brown, Victor E. Colussi, Brian Estey, Cameron Foltz, Daniel Gresh, Reza Haghshenas, Akhil Isanaka, Nikhil Kotibhaskar, Anthony Ransford, Ciarán Ryan-Anderson, Brian Neyenhuis, David Hayes, Tzvetan S. Metodi, Andrew C. Potter
abstract: Quantum error correction enables scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation by suppressing logical errors exponentially with code distance once physical error rates fall below a critical threshold. Here we demonstrate below-threshold operation of triangular color codes with distances $d=3,5,$ and $7$ on Quantinuum's Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. Leveraging both circuit- and hardware- level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as $5_{-2}^{+4}\times 10^{-6}$, and demonstrate error suppression by over an order of magnitude, $Λ=12_{-2}^{+3}$, with each successive increase in code distance. Moreover, we demonstrate below threshold scaling of error rates for Clifford two-qubit randomized benchmarking circuits when encoded in $d=3,5$ color codes, achieving logical error rate of $7^{+3}_{-3}\times 10^{-5}$ per logical two-qubit Clifford at distance $5$ with a suppression factor of $Λ=9_{-3}^{+8}$. We compare logical performance for existing near-optimal algorithmic decoders, and both convolutional neural network and transformer-based neural network decoders capable of real-time decoding an order of magnitude faster than the syndrome extraction rate. These results approach the logical error rates required for megaquop-scale quantum computation and indicate that scaled trapped-ion processors could reach application-relevant performance with substantially smaller code blocks than indicated by previous results in other qubit modalities.
summary: This research demonstrates that quantum error correction using triangular color codes can operate significantly below the theoretical error threshold on a trapped-ion quantum processor. By combining hardware leakage mitigation with advanced neural network decoding, the authors achieved extremely low logical error rates. These results suggest that trapped-ion systems can reach application-relevant performance with smaller code blocks than previously thought necessary.
main_problem: The paper demonstrates quantum error correction (QEC) operation well below the theoretical threshold to enable scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_result: They achieved logical error rates as low as $5 	imes 10^{-6}$ and demonstrated error suppression by over an order of magnitude ($\Lambda \approx 12$) when increasing the code distance.
method: The study combines hardware-level leakage reduction schemes with advanced machine learning decoders (CNN and Transformer) to process syndrome measurements from color codes.
model_or_system: The work uses triangular color codes on Quantinuum's Helios trapped-ion quantum processor, which utilizes $^{137}	ext{Ba}^+$ ions as qubits.
key_observables: Logical Error Rate (LER), Suppression Factor ($\Lambda$), and performance of various decoders (Tesseract, CNN, RTT).
important_parameters: Code distances $d=3, 5, 7$; physical error rates ($p$) relative to the threshold ($p_{	ext{th}}$).
main_assumptions: The hardware-level scheme was limited to three cycles, and the neural network decoders were applied without further fine-tuning on hardware data.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the color code structure, the syndrome extraction circuit, and plots showing the distance scaling of the logical error rate.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup on the trapped-ion platform, presents results from memory and randomized benchmarking experiments, and provides extensive technical details on training and implementing CNN and Transformer decoders.
why_interesting: The combination of physical implementation on trapped ions with state-of-the-art ML decoding techniques pushes the boundaries of achievable error suppression, providing concrete benchmarks for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
